findings: The complete November guide and May guide describe Dashboard Acceptance-page suggestions, not automatic optimization actions: an account may show zero to three, based on settings, integration and thresholds; Stripe refreshes them daily and the merchant can dismiss or send feedback (old raw lines 8-20; new raw lines 9-21). Estimated impacts and recommendation outcomes are not guaranteed, may have cost/fraud/legal tradeoffs, and require business decision (old raw line 14; new raw line 15).

Both captures allow estimated revenue/payment-volume increase OR fraud-model improvement, with revenue increases displayed in settlement currency (old raw lines 22-26; new raw lines 23-27). Annualized revenue estimates use recent-month all or relevant volume multiplied by an average uplift and 12, assuming stable volume; the average comes from other businesses and relevant-volume estimates exclude inapplicable payments (old raw lines 28-34; new raw lines 29-33). Current source line 13 and related concept line 77 incorrectly imply each recommendation has an annual revenue estimate, so correct this baseline overstatement separately from the navigation/format delta.

The NTID recommendation applies to an off-session merchant-initiated transaction using a previous on-session transaction or validation from the same customer, especially when Stripe did not authorize the underlying card previously or card numbers are used without a Stripe Customer object. Stripe says it handles NTIDs automatically if all payments pass through Stripe; for other processors it might lack the ID unless supplied at PaymentIntent creation (old raw lines 36-45; new raw lines 35-44). Source line 26 should retain the same-customer, mixed-processor and automatic-handling conditions rather than implying every MIT requires a manual NTID.

Other recommendations remain: share postal codes for Visa credit AVS and potentially favorable US interchange; disable the two blunt AVS/CVC Radar blocks, optionally use risk-score variants while highest-risk automatic blocking remains; reduce manual 3DS requests on low-risk transactions outside regions with authentication requirements; investigate high 3DS abandonment (old raw lines 47-84; new raw lines 46-83). The source's five-row table broadly covers these at lines 22-35, but its 'SCA regions' shorthand must not imply all payments in a region require 3DS or that all fraud checks should be disabled (new raw lines 52-79).

Neither captured page specifies a recommendation acceptance API, observed authorization gain, processor settlement, actual fraud-model result or merchant-specific compliance decision. API versus Dashboard 3DS request controls are separate, and stopping optional requests does not affect payments that require 3DS by regulation (old raw lines 69-80; new raw lines 68-79). findings: Cash balance and invoice balance remain distinct: unreconciled or excess bank-transfer funds enter the customer's per-currency cash balance for later payments to that same customer or return up to the available amount; it cannot be directly topped up or used as a wallet. Invoice balance is a liability/credit offset for future invoices, adjusted by Customer Balance Transactions, not spendable cash (old raw lines 8-20; new raw lines 9-21; source lines 17-19).

Viewing cash balance still means retrieving a Customer and expanding cash_balance, or viewing the Customer page. A customer-configured Account in Accounts v2 is addressed through the Customers API with its acct_ ID as path parameter; the new capture adds generally available Accounts v2 for Connect users versus public preview for others, with preview-version specification for preview participants. Do not collapse the v1 Customer and customer-configured Account identities or infer universal availability (old raw lines 22-37, 113; new raw lines 23-38, 123; source line 21).

Paying from available cash balance still uses a customer_balance PaymentIntent and sufficient funds; insufficient funds cause failure, with separate bank-transfer funding as a route for more funds. The new page explicitly says to enable bank transfers in Dashboard before intent creation, and its curl examples distinguish customer_account for Accounts v2 from customer for Customers v1. PaymentIntent creation/confirm=true and return_url in the illustrative request do not independently prove success or a redirect requirement; check actual intent state (old raw lines 115-165; new raw lines 125-167; source lines 23-33).

The seven cash-balance transaction types and their causes are unchanged: funded, applied_to_payment, unapplied_from_payment, refunded_from_payment, return_initiated, return_canceled and transferred_to_balance. Funded may auto-apply depending on reconciliation; return_initiated is not completed bank return, and transferred_to_balance refers to failed returns/insufficient details, not a merchant top-up path (old raw lines 167-185; new raw lines 169-187; source lines 35-45).

findings: The May 11 and November 7 guides share the same core integration: request Stripe forwarding access, collect card details with Payment Element, create a Stripe PaymentMethod on the client with manual creation, send its ID to a merchant server, and make a server-side ForwardingRequest to a configured third-party destination (old raw lines 8-17, 21-105, 189-260; new raw lines 9-13, 27-29, 33-118, 197-263). Neither a PaymentMethod nor the ForwardingRequest itself is a Stripe PaymentIntent, destination authorization, capture, or settlement outcome.

November adds an explicit client/Stripe/server/processor sequence diagram. It says Stripe forwards card data, receives a processor response, redacts identified PCI-sensitive data, and relays that response to the merchant server (new raw lines 15-25; diff lines 10-22). May only had the diagram reference/alt text (old raw line 13). This is a substantive documentation clarification about relay/redaction boundaries, not proof of comprehensive redaction or a successful payment.

The example sets Elements mode payment, amount 1099 USD, paymentMethodCreation manual, calls elements.submit before stripe.createPaymentMethod, and sends only paymentMethod.id to the server in both HTML/JS and React variants (new raw lines 33-118, 121-195; old raw lines 21-107, 109-187). These are client collection/validation and PaymentMethod creation steps; the actual processor request is separate and server-owned.

The server example requires a support-configured destination/test endpoint, uses the PaymentMethod ID, destination URL, destination API and idempotency headers, JSON amount/reference and blank card fields, and replacements for number/expiry/CVC/name (new raw lines 197-242; old raw lines 189-240). The example checks response_details.status, parses response_details.body on its 200 branch, and catches errors; its client handler checks error versus status (new raw lines 244-279; old raw lines 242-277). Request shape, response branch and status 200 are examples, not evidence the destination accepted or processed a charge.

The mapped source line 21 says 'Stripe always returns 200' without a condition and next to the response_details.status check. The related retained Vault and Forward guide says the API returns 200 for any response from the destination endpoint, even a destination 400, with destination response/error in response.body (raw/stripe-vault-and-forward-2026.md lines 748-756; wiki/sources/source-stripe-vault-and-forward.md line 37). That statement does not say Stripe requests cannot fail; this guide catches errors and checks response_details.status (new raw lines 244-257). Qualify the source and reciprocal concept line 23 to destination-response handling, and do not conflate HTTP response, response_details.status and a successful processor payment.

Payment Element can create a PaymentMethod; a custom frontend may create one directly. Server submits PaymentMethod ID, URL, header/body and replacements. The demo endpoint and pm_card_visa are test fixtures, not production vault or authorization proof (raw/stripe-payments-forwarding-token-vault-2026-11-07.md:26-46; raw/stripe-forwarding-token-vault-2026.md:15-43). The sample bearer token is embedded only in the demo example and must not be treated as an account secret or production credential.

Vault must have valid PCI Attestation of Compliance refreshed annually, HTTPS JSON request/response, a single static configured URL, header-based authentication with every request, additional headers preconfigured with Stripe support, no client certificates, and 15-second request timeout (raw/stripe-payments-forwarding-token-vault-2026-11-07.md:48-72,115-119; raw/stripe-forwarding-token-vault-2026.md:45-69,112-116). The body example has card number/expiry/name/CVC and optional metadata; decrypted values are inserted only for fields present in the request body. CVC is available only for the first API request to Stripe after tokenization; Stripe removes it from its system after a short period, and the vault/merchant must not store it (new raw lines 74-105; old raw lines 71-102). The vault need not return a body; if it does, Stripe relays it and forbids sensitive fields. The response-code prose says 'same response code' but its concrete example says upstream 400 yields Forwarding API HTTP 200 with upstream 400/error in body (raw/stripe-payments-forwarding-token-vault-2026-11-07.md:107-113; raw/stripe-forwarding-token-vault-2026.md:104-110).
